changes.text: How many terms of the AP $33, 30, 27, \dots$ must be taken so that their sum is $135$? Explain why there are two answers, and verify them.
changes.answer:
$a = 33$, $d = -3$. $S_{n} = \frac{n}{2}[66 + (n - 1)(-3)] = \frac{n}{2}(69 - 3n) = 135$.
So $69n - 3n^{2} = 270$, i.e. $n^{2} - 23n + 90 = 0$, so $(n - 5)(n - 18) = 0$ and $n = 5$ or $n = 18$.
Check for $n = 5$: $33 + 30 + 27 + 24 + 21 = 135$.
The terms keep decreasing, reach zero and then become negative: $a_{6} = 18$, $a_{7} = 15$, $\dots$, $a_{12} = 0$, $\dots$, $a_{18} = 33 + 17 \times (-3) = -18$. The 6th to 18th terms are $18, 15, \dots, 3, 0, -3, \dots, -18$; they cancel in pairs, so their sum is 0 and the sum of the first 18 terms is again 135.
Answer: 5 terms or 18 terms.

changes.text: For what value of $n$ are the $n$th terms of the APs $41, 44, 47, \dots$ and $5, 10, 15, \dots$ equal?
changes.answer: $n$th term of the first AP $= 41 + (n - 1)3$; $n$th term of the second AP $= 5 + (n - 1)5$. Equating: $41 + 3(n - 1) = 5 + 5(n - 1)$, so $2(n - 1) = 36$, $n - 1 = 18$, $n = 19$. (Both 19th terms are $95$.)

changes.text: A circular park has centre $O$ and radius $15\text{ m}$. A straight road touches the boundary of the park at $T$. A lamp post $P$ stands on the road, $20\text{ m}$ from $T$. A second straight road from $P$ also touches the park, at $S$.
changes.answer: (i) $90^\circ$; (ii) $OP = 25\text{ m}$; (iii) $TS = 24\text{ m}$, OR area of $OTPS = 300\text{ m}^{2}$.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: What is the measure of the angle between the radius $OT$ and the road?
parts.answer: The road is a tangent at $T$, so it is perpendicular to the radius $OT$: the angle is $90^\circ$.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: Find the distance $OP$ of the lamp post from the centre of the park.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.text: Find the length of the chord $TS$ joining the two points of contact. OR Find the area of quadrilateral $OTPS$.
parts.answer: $PS = PT = 20\text{ m}$ and $OP$ bisects $TS$ at right angles at $M$. Area of $\triangle OTP = \frac{1}{2} \times 15 \times 20 = 150 = \frac{1}{2} \times 25 \times TM$, so $TM = 12\text{ m}$ and $TS = 24\text{ m}$. OR: $\triangle OTP \cong \triangle OSP$, so area of $OTPS = 2 \times 150 = 300\text{ m}^{2}$.

changes.answer: (i) $90^\circ$; (ii) $OP = 29\text{ m}$; (iii) perimeter $82\text{ m}$, area $420\text{ m}^{2}$.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: Find $\angle OTP$.
parts.answer: The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so $\angle OTP = 90^\circ$.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: Find the distance $OP$.

parts.text: Find the perimeter and the area of quadrilateral $OTPS$.
parts.answer: $PS = PT = 21\text{ m}$ and $OS = OT = 20\text{ m}$, so the perimeter is $2(20 + 21) = 82\text{ m}$. $OTPS$ splits into two congruent right triangles, so area $= 2 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 21 = 420\text{ m}^{2}$.

corrections.originalText: Prove that $\sqrt{5}$ is irrational.

changes.answer: Suppose $\sqrt{5}$ is rational. Then $\sqrt{5} = \frac{a}{b}$ where $a$, $b$ are integers, $b \ne 0$, and $a$, $b$ are co-prime. Squaring, $a^{2} = 5b^{2}$, so 5 divides $a^{2}$. Since 5 is prime, 5 divides $a$. Write $a = 5c$ for some integer $c$. Then $25c^{2} = 5b^{2}$, so $b^{2} = 5c^{2}$. Hence 5 divides $b^{2}$, and so 5 divides $b$. Now 5 is a common factor of $a$ and $b$, which contradicts that they are co-prime. So $\sqrt{5}$ is irrational.

changes.text: A conical vessel of base radius $3 \text{ cm}$ and height $10 \text{ cm}$ is full of water. Spherical lead shots, each of radius $0.5 \text{ cm}$, are dropped into it one by one, and when they are all inside, two-fifths of the water has flowed out. changes.answer:
Volume of water in the cone $= \frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2} h = \frac{1}{3}\pi \times 9 \times 10 = 30\pi \text{ cm}^{3}$.
Water that flows out $= \frac{2}{5} \times 30\pi = 12\pi \text{ cm}^{3}$.

changes.text: Case study: A surveyor wants the width of a canal without crossing it. A tree $T$ stands on the far bank. She marks the point $P$ on the near bank directly opposite the tree, so $PT$ is perpendicular to the bank. She walks along the bank to $Q$ with $PQ = 36\text{ m}$, and fixes a peg $R$ on $PQ$ with $PR = 24\text{ m}$. At $Q$ she turns at a right angle, away from the canal, and walks to a point $U$ from which the peg $R$ and the tree $T$ are in one line. She measures $QU = 9\text{ m}$.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: Name the criterion by which $\triangle PRT \sim \triangle QRU$.
parts.answer: $\angle P = \angle Q = 90^\circ$ and $\angle PRT = \angle QRU$ (vertically opposite), so the triangles are similar by the AA criterion.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: Find the ratio $PR : RQ$ and hence the ratio $TR : RU$.
parts.answer: $RQ = 36 - 24 = 12\text{ m}$, so $PR : RQ = 24 : 12 = 2 : 1$. By similarity $TR : RU = PR : RQ = 2 : 1$.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.text: Find the width of the canal and the distance $TU$.
parts.answer: $\frac{PT}{QU} = \frac{PR}{RQ} = 2$, so $PT = 18\text{ m}$, the width of the canal. In right $\triangle QRU$, $RU = \sqrt{12^{2} + 9^{2}} = 15\text{ m}$, so $TR = 30\text{ m}$ and $TU = 30 + 15 = 45\text{ m}$.

changes.answer: (i) AA; (ii) $PR : RQ = TR : RU = 2 : 1$; (iii) width $18\text{ m}$, $TU = 45\text{ m}$.

A school is installing a vertical flag mast on level ground. To estimate its height, Meera, who is $1.5\text{ m}$ tall, stands upright near the mast. At that moment her shadow is $2\text{ m}$ long while the shadow of the mast is $12\text{ m}$ long. (i) Name the similarity criterion by which the triangle formed by Meera and her shadow is similar to the triangle formed by the mast and its shadow. [1]
(ii) Find the height of the mast. [1]
(iii) The wire is fixed to the ground at a point $12\text{ m}$ from the foot of the mast. Find the length of the wire. [2]

changes.text: A school is installing a vertical flag mast on level ground. To estimate its height, Meera, who is $1.5\text{ m}$ tall, stands upright near the mast. At that moment her shadow is $2\text{ m}$ long while the shadow of the mast is $12\text{ m}$ long. The mast will be held by a steel wire fixed to its top and to a point on the ground in line with the mast's base.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: Name the similarity criterion by which the triangle formed by Meera and her shadow is similar to the triangle formed by the mast and its shadow.
parts.answer: The sun's rays strike at the same angle, so the angles of elevation are equal; each triangle also has a right angle (person and mast are vertical). Hence the triangles are similar by AA similarity.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: Find the height of the mast.
parts.answer: Let the height be $h$. By similarity, $\frac{h}{1.5} = \frac{12}{2}$, so $h = 1.5 \times 6 = 9\text{ m}$.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.text: The wire is fixed to the ground at a point $12\text{ m}$ from the foot of the mast. Find the length of the wire. OR A second wire is fixed to a point on the mast $6\text{ m}$ above the ground and to a ground point $8\text{ m}$ from the foot of the mast. Find the length of this wire.
parts.answer: The mast, the ground and the wire form a right triangle with legs $9\text{ m}$ and $12\text{ m}$, so the wire length $= \sqrt{9^{2} + 12^{2}} = \sqrt{225} = 15\text{ m}$. OR: length $= \sqrt{6^{2} + 8^{2}} = \sqrt{100} = 10\text{ m}$.

changes.answer: (i) AA; (ii) $9\text{ m}$; (iii) $15\text{ m}$ (OR $10\text{ m}$).

(i) Find the ratio of the sides of the two fields. [1]
(ii) Show that field $ABC$ is right-angled and name the vertex of the right angle. [1]
(iii) Find the area of field $PQR$ and the cost of fencing it at ₹50 per metre. [2]

changes.text: Case study: A farmer owns two triangular fields, $ABC$ and $PQR$, with $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$. The sides of field $ABC$ are $AB = 9\text{ m}$, $BC = 12\text{ m}$ and $CA = 15\text{ m}$. The longest side $PR$ of field $PQR$ is $25\text{ m}$.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: Find the ratio of the sides of the two fields.
parts.answer: $CA$ and $PR$ are the corresponding longest sides, so the ratio of sides is $\frac{CA}{PR} = \frac{15}{25} = \frac{3}{5}$, i.e. $3 : 5$.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: Show that field $ABC$ is right-angled and name the vertex of the right angle.
parts.answer: $AB^{2} + BC^{2} = 81 + 144 = 225 = CA^{2}$, so by the converse of Pythagoras theorem the angle opposite $CA$ is a right angle, i.e. at $B$.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.text: Find the area of field $PQR$ and the cost of fencing it at ₹50 per metre.
parts.answer: Sides of $PQR$: $PQ = \frac{5}{3} \times 9 = 15\text{ m}$, $QR = \frac{5}{3} \times 12 = 20\text{ m}$, $PR = 25\text{ m}$. Since $\angle Q = \angle B = 90^\circ$, area $= \frac{1}{2} \times 15 \times 20 = 150\text{ m}^{2}$. Perimeter $= 15 + 20 + 25 = 60\text{ m}$, so fencing costs $60 \times 50 =$ ₹3000.

changes.answer: (i) $3 : 5$; (ii) right angle at $B$; (iii) area $150\text{ m}^{2}$, fencing cost ₹3000.

LHS $= \sin^{2}\theta + 2\sin\theta\operatorname{cosec}\theta + \operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta + 2\cos\theta\sec\theta + \sec^{2}\theta$.
Since $\sin\theta\operatorname{cosec}\theta = 1$ and $\cos\theta\sec\theta = 1$, LHS $= (\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta) + 4 + \operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta + \sec^{2}\theta = 1 + 4 + \operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta + \sec^{2}\theta$.
Using $\operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta = 1 + \cot^{2}\theta$ and $\sec^{2}\theta = 1 + \tan^{2}\theta$: LHS $= 5 + 1 + \cot^{2}\theta + 1 + \tan^{2}\theta = 7 + \tan^{2}\theta + \cot^{2}\theta$ = RHS. Hence proved.

(Use $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$)
changes.answer:
Let $F$ be the foot and $T$ the top of the lighthouse, $FT = 80\text{ m}$. The angle of depression of a boat equals its angle of elevation from the boat (alternate angles).
Nearer boat $A$ (depression $45^\circ$): $\tan 45^\circ = \frac{80}{FA}$, so $FA = 80\text{ m}$.
Farther boat $B$ (depression $30^\circ$): $\tan 30^\circ = \frac{80}{FB}$, so $FB = 80\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$.
Distance between the boats $= FB - FA = 80\sqrt{3} - 80 = 80(\sqrt{3} - 1) = 80 \times 0.732 = 58.56\text{ m}$.
Answer: $58.56\text{ m}$

parts.label: (ii)

parts.answer: $60^\circ$. The horizontal line through the top of the block is parallel to the ground, so the angle of depression and the angle of elevation are alternate angles and are equal.
